story_text.value:
EtherPK (a markdown / wikilink based notes app) tasks are plain markdown, but the EtherPK client has built powerful functionality on top of markdown tasks, integrating a Kanban board and MCP server to allow you to manage your work in your notes and easily hand off with instruction and full task context to your AI Agent (e.g. Claude Code).

A task in is a markdown checkbox line in your notes, written in any document, wherever and whenever the task or idea comes up. If you nest it under another task and it becomes that task's subtask. A Kanban board shows those lines as cards and keeps no copy of them, so moving a card edits the line. The task editor is a form over the same text, so a picture, a comment or a subtask you add there ends up as text in the note.

Full post at: https://blog.etherpk.com/hand-your-markdown-tasks-to-claude-...

This is part of my experiment to see if I can build a SaaS in an agentic world.

I've been wanting to put something out in the wild for a while. I think that although we have agents that can build stuff and deploy it to any hosting solution, we still need to be assured that the system is available and working.

Although I've started with a very thin product, I'm solo building this out to support a few use-cases that I think might be quite cool.

Under-the-hood I've actually used Elixir to help make things more stable and robust.

Appreciate feedback and hopefully people will follow along with my journey.

story_text.value:
Hello HN!

I wrote a browser extension (also available as a userscript) that allows to insert quotes into site's reply message box using selected text + hitting 'r' (as it's done on Github). It targets only specific sites (basecamp.com, slack.com), because that's what we use at our company daily.

The idea came out of my boss (who's also a good friend of mine) frustration. He always complained that Basecamp's replies are so inconvenient compared to Github's way. You have to select the quote, copy it into clipboard, then scroll to the reply box, paste it, then select the text again, and finally format it as a quote using editor's toolbar. That's 6 steps vs 2 on Github!

Last summer Basecamp rolled out a new facelift featuring a heavy usage of keyboard shortcuts. But "reply with r" was still missing, so another rant from my boss followed :)

At that time I was toying with an old browser extension written long time ago as a learning project. I was rewriting it against the new extension API to see what changed/improved. Being immersed into the topic, it was obvious that a thought about "fixing" Basecamp with a browser extension came into my head.

So I started working on the Dial R for Reply project during my spare time. I had two clear motivations: 1. I knew it would make someone's life better (myself included). 2. I would learn something new along the way.

During the process I realised I could also "fix" Slack replies. It was a bit of trial and error (I didn't use any LLMs for reasons stated above). The hardest part was to dig into each editor's public and private APIs (Basecamp uses lexical, Slack uses Quill). I had to resort to using internals, so be warned -- it might break when site owners decided to update those libraries. On the other hand, hacking a site with an extension is a risky operation anyway (anything may be changed at any time).

Key takeaways:

1. browser extensions are cool! Compared to native apps and electron wrappers, you as a customer have such a powerful tool to amend a web application as you like. 2. if you are a library writer, if possible, keep your private state and/or functions accessible to the outside world. Yes, you should clearly mark them as a private, so there's a clear boundary drawn between what can be used safely and what's not. But being able to peek into private state was the only option for me to debug and hack into the application.

story_text.value:
I wanted to see if a speech model could spell a name better if it heard it, not just read it.

Most STT tools handle custom words as text (keyterm list, fixing transcript after with llm, etc).

So I trained an adapter to try it, specifically a LoRA on Qwen3-ASR 1.7b (see benchmark). This LoRA transcribes words only after it hears a recording of each of your custom words.

To make this model easier to use in day-to-day life, we also built Detail Keeper. It's a Mac app where you can put this adapter to use by specifying difficult-to-transcribe-correctly words and then having them picked up correctly in your recordings.

We've found this helpful in two specific cases: 1. Words STT has never heard: invented characters and places, codenames, unusual surnames. 2. Your spelling of a word it does know: Kathryn and not Catherine, Jon and not John.

I wasn't able to achieve both good recognition and recognizing many words (1k+) with the model alone.

Detail Keeper first narrows each passage to the likeliest taught names by sound. Then the adapter writes the passage, and the app checks it against a plain transcript.

On our open benchmark (audiobooks, 1,100 name mentions) it spells taught names as well as Eleven Labs Scribe with keyterms: 89.6% vs 88.2%, no measurable difference. The only downside is that it overwrites a few more untaught names and changes slightly more ordinary words.

Everything, including where we lose, is at detailkeeper.com/benchmark.

Note: It's free, local and nothing leaves your Mac, but it does require an Apple M series+ mac and OS 26+ currently. Also worth noting that it downloads about 3.6GB of models and only works in English right now.

If you're interested, you can also find the adapter itself on HF: huggingface.co/virgil-coach/own-names-qwen3-asr

story_text.value:
Some of you will remember lofiatc.com and I was a huge fan and heavy user until it got shut down. It was streaming LiveATC feeds, and when those got cut off the site went dark and has been ever since.

So I decided to bring it back in a way that wouldn't fall to the same fate. I've been an ATC nerd for years (ever since you could still listen to the radio on the arm rest of commercial flights) so this summer I rented a Fiat 500, stuck an airband antenna on the roof, and spent a day driving to three Chicago airports with my laptop in the passenger seat to record the audio I needed in person. This took me to the viewing area at Chicago Executive (KPWK), the cell phone lot at O'Hare (KORD), and the top of a parking garage at Midway (KMDW). The whole chain was a Bingfu mag-mount antenna connected to an airband filter and then to an RTL-SDR, all captured via SDR++.

If you're interested, you can read a full post on how the recording day came together here: https://finalapproach.fm/field-notes/chicago-recording-day/

Once I had all the audio, I layered it on top of lo-fi tracks and created one "album" per airport, each with its own vibe. Each track is named after something unique to that airport or something we heard on the radio, and I've had it on as background music for work for about two months now, which is why I built it in the first place!

Also important to me was putting this out there in the world with no signup required and no ads. Just like on the original site, finalapproach.fm gives you two sliders that let you push the radio up or the music up depending on which you want to hear more of. And there are pre-built mixes on YouTube and all your favorite music streaming services (search for Final Approach Radio).

Happy to answer questions about the radio side, the legal side (as much as I can, obviously), or the editing (largely done with Claude Code).

story_text.value:
I’ve been doing a lot of solo development lately and found myself hitting Claude token limits halfway through the week constantly. Even with a Max plan, I’d have to switch over to Codex or Cursor, and it would be a bit difficult to get used to the nuances of each harness.

It’s still a problem for me, but I finally built Thinker to save me some tokens and help me get a bit more out of my coding agent subscriptions.

I started off a bit in the dark about how token billing works, and had to dig deeper to figure out what workflows ended up hurting my budget the most. By far, it was large context windows. Claude tries to help out on costs by offering prompt caching - which is sort of a bandage on the bigger problem: context bloat.

I find that my context window gets bloated with unneeded tokens in two main ways:

Tool outputs from subtasks that are long finished. File reads, Bash commands, MCP outputs, etc. Main idea is that the model finished the work but carries the weight of it for every subsequent call - translating to wasted token usage. CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md getting way too big. Lots of content gets dumped into these files as your agents work in your repo. I found that it’s not clear what is actually useful to be included there. Every token here counts, because it will be paid for in every session, and its cost scales linearly with the duration of your session.

Thinker addresses both of these issues. We have a proxy that wires in between your harness and model to cut out old context that we determine is no longer needed for your current task. Based on the provider you’re using, we determine the right time to batch enough context to cut that justifies the cache re-write cost, which gets paid off after X subsequent calls.

We also analyze your sessions and figure out which parts of your instruction files don’t really get used - and send you suggestions to cut or compress those sections. Thinker will kick off a subagent to do that work for you and open a PR you can review.

Finally, we use your sessions to record knowledge notes by distilling your sessions with a cheap model (Haiku, Luna). These notes are then served at prompt time via a cross-encoder, also on your machine, that decides whether a note is relevant to the user’s prompt.

Here are some data points to show how exactly Thinker saves you coding agent costs: https://thinker.sh/see-the-data

If you’re hitting problems at all with usage limits, it’d be great to hear how you’ve been trying to mitigate it.

Our open-source repo here (MIT License): https://github.com/yoavshmariahu/thinker

story_text.value:
Glad to showcase SKI (https://justski.it) , a voice-first coding harness.

It supports multiple agents from different providers, just like conductor used to. You can run claude code, codex, antigravity etc. You can also add multiple subscriptions of Claude code or others, which will automatically switch when the limits are hit so that you can continue working on projects seamlessly

Voice first - You can talk to it, and it will talk back and keep you updated on tasks and status. You could also ask it to speak only when needed and it will adapt. (It doesn't read out the code line by line, unless you specifically ask it to). It is multilingual and supports 80+ languages. It can automatically convert the audio in your language to English for the models to work on. There is a optional review window if you need to verify it before sending to the agents.

Chain reactions: Maybe you need one agent to do a task, and then hand it over to the next agent. We call it chain. And you can just do it using voice easily in SKI.

Lives in notch (can be hidden behind notch as well, but also has a bigger UI like conductor)

Different voice for different sessions: Distinguish projects by voice.

Can take screenshots if you ask it to (will show flash)

One agent for all - Experimental feature where a single agent manages multiple sessions by voice, routing your requests on its own and keeping track of tasks across different sessions.

UI pop ups for things that need your attention - When in notch, agents will pop up options and explain what each options are, when they need an input from you. For instance, if there are 3 options for some task, the UI will show the 3 tasks as a floating window, which you can either click or choose by voice. Agents will also explain by voice if needed.

Floating taskbar like a widget - Floats when enabled, showing all tasks in different sessions and different agents, along with current progress and step. Can give voice inputs by just clicking on them and talking.

Loops - available for all agents as a harness tool

Computer use - Stays in notch and does without interfering your work.

Git integrated: Can create sessions from PR, merge, see comments etc. All by voice, text and UI buttons. Also custom branch names with configurable prefix.

Pricing: Text usage - Unlimited, free forever, No limits Voice: Free 300 credits per month.

Hi everyone,

I built Lunar to make my day to day work on our AI gateway easier: basic testing of different providers, advanced testing of features like complexity router, and so on. Lunar allows you to easily switch across providers, gives you debugging tools (`/debug` to dump provider response headers, `/request` to dump the current prompt as a curl request, easy configuration with Lua, and more...).

You can use your OpenAI or xAI subscription on it (Anthropic also supported, but use it at your own risk, as it's against Anthropic's terms - I developed it as an experimente). API keys also supported.

Eager to know your thoughts! :)

story_text.value:
When I started working hands-on with OpenAPI specifications, it became clear very quickly that using an editor to read large volumes of deeply nested JSON sucks, a very great deal. So I went looking for something to help, and came across https://jless.io This is an awesome terminal app for navigating nasty JSON documents. I am forever indebted to Paul Martinez for writing this tool.

But it did have some gaps. It couldn't reload files that had changed, keeping your place in the JSON structure, which I really needed. And it only loaded one file at a time. But unfortunately it was written in Rust, and I didn't know Rust, and back in the pre-AI days that was kind of a huge blocker.

But of course once we got models that could actually write decent code, the obvious idea came to me - I'll just add my features and submit a PR! Happy days. Except by that stage my requirements had grown - I also needed to handle many other file formats, like CSV, TOML, INI, and even XML. So I got side-tracked extending another side-project - an easy going JSON parser that supported comments, and trailing commas, the usual sort of thing.

During COVID, with a SaaS startup in the events space now on the rocks, I was looking for some distraction and decided to refactor this little easy-going JSON parser of mine. It used a generated parser and was slow. I read some blog posts about how all production-grade language parsers are pretty much hand-crafted recursive descent, and thought, how hard could it be!

Five years later, after many many fun experiments, and production use, I ended up with a runtime parser system: https://tabnas.dev This is a quirky approach to parsing that is partly recursive descent, partly a state machine, and mostly empirical hacking. It works, and it's pretty fast, and I use it for real projects. It has the nice property that grammars are dynamic - you don't generate code, the grammar is executed. A fancy regular expression engine, but revved up to parse anything into a proper abstract syntax tree.

Now with that in hand, I could return to the original project and create my own version of jless that solved the itches I needed to scratch: a watch mode; multiple tabs; load any data format into a tree structure

Now I still don't know Rust. I mean I like the idea, but there are only so many hours in the day. But now we have AI, so now I do get to go to the candy store. Combining jless.io, and tabnas.dev, and my requirements, I built (caused to be built?), aless - the less for any format!

Now this is also a nice stress test for the tabnas parsing engine, and I was very pleased about that too.

So if you need to review lots of data structure files on the command line, and need a terminal app to do so, this is for you. I can't help but be struck by the irony however that the need for such a thing is much less now - I mostly get agents to look at large JSON documents now. Still, our puny human brains need help sometimes, and this lets me review documents when I need to.

It is also really nice and satisfying to see how easy it is to now bring together open source components to create what is essentially personal software.

But I think the key thing out of this little project is that the basic physics of software development remain the same. Software should be built from components glued together. Components should have well-defined interfaces. Aim to reduce cognitive load - this is useful to both humans and machines.

Yes, the entire thing could be built from scratch, using a textual specification, and be a mire of over-engineered AI slop, and still be perfectly usable. But the way I actually built it, with AI as a coding companion, using components was deeply satisfying because I still understand the essence of the code, while being able to ignore the accidental complexity. Components give you another layer of abstraction with fewer things to think about, and that allows your human mind to stay in the game.

story_text.value:
A WYSIWYG rich Markdown editor for VS Code.

I use agent a lot for planning, and there is not so much real beautiful and confortable Markdown editor. It gets better but i needed several special things: first-class frontmatter with validation, Sphinx MyST edition, in-cell table edition and do not kill my raw text formatting.

I hope the rendering is extra-clean, allowing to edit a paragraph or a admonition. It supports mermaid, plantuml, vega/vega-lite graph without extern dependencies. It also supports all Sphinx MyST and GitHub Flavored Markdown. I also like the custom "radio choice" similar to GFM tick, really useful for decision making directly in Markdown. I use it as an active working document with my agents and later as a rich collaborative surface in small team. HTML artifacts are amazing with coding agents, but heavy, cannot be displayed as it in Gitlab/Github file, and cannot easily keep states such as choices or micro edition.

It is also used to be a great frontmatter editor OKF Schema that gives a JSONSchema to a frontmatter for OpenKnownledge Format document.

title.value: Show HN: Markdown OKF-Schema Studio for VS Code
